https://www.mediafax.ro/english/romania-.text: Romania “counts” its wild birds: project worth over 49 million lei, running until 2029 The Ministry of Environment, Waters and Forests announced the signing of the financing contract for the project “Strengthening the national management and monitoring system of bird species in Romania”, with a total value of over 49 million lei. Of this amount, approximately 41.7 million lei represents co-financing from European Union funds. The project is financed through the Sustainable Development Program 2021-2027 and runs from 2025-2029. The main objective is to improve the system through which Romania monitors and reports on the status of bird species of community interest. The authorities thus aim to obtain complete and updated information on their conservation status. Birds will be monitored directly on the ground An important component of the project is the activity carried out on the ground. Specialists will monitor species of community interest, and the information obtained will subsequently be collected and analyzed at national level. Based on this data, the Country Report on the conservation status of bird species will also be developed. However, the project is not limited to the inventory and analysis of populations. Conservation measures are to be developed for species considered at risk, and the program also includes information and awareness activities aimed at the public. Ministry of Environment: Protecting nature begins with accurate data The ministry emphasizes that Romania hosts some of the most important populations of wild birds in Europe, and their conservation has a direct role in protecting biodiversity and maintaining the balance of ecosystems. The investment also has a component related to Romania’s European obligations. Improving the national monitoring system should allow authorities to report more accurately on the status of species and base protection measures on updated data. “Nature cannot be protected without accurate data and constant monitoring. That is why we are investing in knowledge, research and conservation, in order to protect bird species and Romania’s natural heritage, in accordance with European standards,” the Ministry of Environment said. The program would thus provide a database and a more detailed picture of the state of bird populations in Romania by 2029, information necessary for establishing future conservation policies. Photograph: Denny Simmons/The Tennessean/Reuters View image in fullscreen A witness, Catherine Sweeney, recounts the failed execution of Christa Pike beside a picture of the murder victim Colleen Slemmer. Photograph: Denny Simmons/The Tennessean/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Christa Pike in ‘critical condition’ as Tennessee halts all executions Failed attempt to execute 50-year-old prompts review of state’s execution practices. Plus the California woman who is allergic to cold Martin Belam Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.59 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Tennessee’s governor has suspended executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says the state’s failed lethal injection execution attempt has left her in a critical condition. Bill Lee, the Republican state governor, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Leading voices on the death penalty in the US have told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings should be halted nationwide . What have Pike’s lawyers said about her condition? Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said: “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care. She is in a critical condition.” What did witnesses say took place during the execution attempt? Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, said : “They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged. She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.” What was Pike convicted of? She was convicted of the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, alongside her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Lee said he had not yet spoken to Slemmer’s family after the failed execution. Family of Renee Good sues administration officials and the ICE agent who shot her View image in fullscreen A screen at a news conference announcing the civil lawsuits. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday. In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers. Why has the DNC issue d a lawsuit against the administration? The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday . “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. Which states are leading the resistance to the Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules? Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule . The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the federal government was showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations would pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution. Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors View image in fullscreen Elon Musk has been given an advisory role in a Pentagon project. Photograph: Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has given extraordinary influence to two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. Luckey, 34, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, unmanned aerial vehicles, and space technology, and has already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare, saying he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through the crust of the Earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. What have been the latest developments with US forces in the Middle East? The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon. Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell View image in fullscreen Letitia James. Photograph: Michael Brochstein/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University . “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.” In other news … View image in fullscreen The Gemini 4 Argon logo. Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Google has rolled out a new Gemini AI model – but has restricted access over safety concerns. California’s attorney general, meanwhile, has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over reports of rogue agents’ hacking. SpaceX launched a crew to the ISS successfully , with Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, making her second trip to the space station. Lawmakers have called for action on what they say are “plainly illegal” taxpayer-funded ads to promote Donald Trump in the run-up to the midterms. The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty , turning down a defense motion. Kanye West’s sold-out Russia concerts have been cancelled , organisers have confirmed. Russia’s foreign ministry had called the planned shows unacceptable due to the rapper’s “glorification” of Adolf Hitler. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/trum.text: US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he had scheduled a call with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to discuss a suspected plague case at a Siberian research institute that has drawn international scrutiny, offering US help while Russian regional officials said they would handle the situation themselves.Trump told reporters at the White House that the call with Putin was scheduled for "very soon" and said "very deep discussions" were under way in Washington on the case.On Monday he had told reporters the US was ready to help, calling plague "a rough disease". "That's a disease we used to be able to control," he said. "We'll help."Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia welcomed the offer of assistance. Yet Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health watchdog, shot back at the US, stating Russia was "ready to assist the United States in tackling outbreaks of infectious diseases," citing measles outbreaks in three US states.Local authorities also rejected outside help, claiming that there is no threat of a plague outbreak in Siberia."We will manage on our own. The situation is under full control. The dangerous diagnosis is not being confirmed, but we are still following all protocol measures," deputy mayor of Shelekhov district Elena Sofina said in a statement, adding that 60% of those placed in quarantine had been released.All quiet in Irkutsk?Darya Shipilova, 28, a researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died in hospital on 2 October. Unconfirmed reports claimed she broke a vial containing a plague pathogen.Official Russian records list the cause of death as "pneumonia of unknown aetiology." Despite negative test results among contacts, authorities quarantined nearly 200 people and placed several hospitals under restrictions, measures inconsistent with ordinary pneumonia.The World Health Organization said on Tuesday it assessed the risk outside Russia as "very low" and saw no signs the disease was spreading. Spokesman Christian Lindmeier said the cause of death had not been officially confirmed and laboratory tests were ongoing.WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organisation had asked Russia for "additional information to determine the cause of the severe pneumonia" and to verify media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unknown cause."Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing in line with the International Health Regulations is critical," he said.The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it was closely monitoring the situation and that "at this time there are no signs of a broader threat to the United States."The US Embassy in Moscow noted it was following the situation and reminded US citizens that the State Department's Level 4 "do not travel" advisory for Russia remains in force.US citizens planning a trip to Russia were again strongly advised not to travel there because of the risk of wrongful detention and security concerns, the embassy said.Residents of Irkutsk told AFP they were not alarmed. "If the situation were really serious, I think by now everything would already have been closed," one man said.Staff at the anti-plague institute have been released from quarantine. The independent outlet Lyudi Baikala published informal comments from colleagues and former classmates of Shipilova casting doubt on the broken-vial account.
